prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most monkey species don't actually cooperate when they search for food. They mostly keep to themselves, and if anything, they try to get the best food for themselves without sharing. That said, there are a few notable exceptions.

The best-known case is the black-and-white ruffed lemur of Madagascar. When a group finds a big haul of fruit, some individuals make a distinctive call that brings other lemurs in, even from other groups. It's one of the few cases of a wild primate calling others to food it could keep for itself.

Some macaques also share food in a more straightforward way. A mother will give pieces of her food to her infants, and in a few species, like the long-tailed macaque, adults will share with unrelated adults they have close relationships with.

When monkeys do communicate about food, they're usually conveying simple things. They may signal that food has been found, where it is, or that it's safe to approach. They don't seem to give detailed descriptions of what the food is like.

So while there are a few cases of food-related cooperation, most monkey communication about food is about locating it and claiming it for oneself.

- During the day. Pick one ordinary activity, like washing your hands, waiting for the kettle to boil, or walking to your car, and do it with full attention. How long do you need for optimal benefits?

- For stress and sleep, research on mindfulness programs like MBSR suggests around 20 to 40 minutes a day, five to seven days a week, over eight weeks produces noticeable changes.
- For everyday calm, even five to ten minutes a day can make a difference within a few weeks, especially if you do it daily.
- The small practices above add up. Three breaths here and there are worth doing even on busy days.

It was the kind of town where everyone knew your mother, and your mother knew everyone's business. Detective Ray Donovan knew it better than most. He'd grown up there, gone to the high school with half the people he'd arrested, and left at twenty-two to get out from under a father who drank too much and raised his hand too often. He came back at forty-five in a dark suit that never quite dried, called in by the state police because the county couldn't pay a full-time detective and didn't know how to ask for one.

The first body was found in the bed of a pickup truck in a cornfield off Highway 23. A woman in her thirties, dressed for work, a white blouse already soaked through with rain. Ray knew her. Her name was Margo Pell, and she'd worked the counter at the diner on Main Street for fifteen years. She smiled at everyone, even the guys who paid in singles and asked for extra sauce.

Ray stood at the tape with his hands in his pockets. The county coroner was still twenty minutes away. Behind him, someone laughed, too loudly for the rain. Ray didn't turn around. He knew it was Terry Boyle, who ran the bait shop and told stories about the war that got longer every year.

"She ain't nothing but a hooker," Terry said.

Ray turned slowly. "You knew her, Terry?"

"Everyone knew her. She gave me a soda once for my nephew. That don't make her a lady."

Ray looked back at the truck. He'd learned a long time ago that how people talked about the dead told you more than what they said to your face. Margo Pell had a sister in Sparta, and a son who was twenty and still lived with her. Ray wrote down Terry's words and didn't write down his own, which were that Terry knew exactly where she'd been before she got into that truck, and that Terry had been working the night shift at the bait shop the night she died.

The second body was found three weeks later, in the same cornfield, in the same bed of a pickup truck. This time it was a man, a construction worker named Dale Haines who had a drinking problem and a wife who was tired of it. Ray didn't tell anyone about the connection to the first case. He didn't tell his captain, he didn't tell the state troopers, and he didn't tell himself. He just started going back through the old files.

There were three bodies in the county ledger from 1998 to 2001 that had never been solved. Two women and a man, all found in the same cornfield, all in the back of a pickup truck, all with no one ever found who had anything to do with it. Ray had been a rookie then, fresh off the academy, and he'd been assigned to the third case because he was the newest and nobody else wanted it. He'd left the case cold, not because he didn't care but because he'd been drunk for six of those months. That was the story he told himself, and he told it often enough that he almost believed it.

Now he went through the old files at night, in his kitchen, with the house dark around him. He had a bottle of bourbon on the counter, next to the files, and he drank from the bottle straight, because a glass was for people who had someone to pour the drink for.

On the fourth page of the third file, he found it. A photo of a woman holding a baby, taken at the county fair. The woman was smiling, and she was wearing a red sweater. The caption said "Volunteer, Oakhaven Fair, 1999." Ray knew that sweater. He'd seen it on a woman at the fair every year since. It was knitted by a woman named Elsie, who ran the craft table and gave away the prizes she'd won. Elsie knew everyone in Oakhaven. She knew who'd been drinking too much, who was on drugs, who had a secret, and she knew it all with a straight face.

Ray drove to the fairgrounds the next morning. The craft hall was empty except for Elsie, who was washing her hands at the sink in the back.

"You've been asking about the fair," she said. She didn't look up.

Ray leaned against the doorframe. "You knew Margo Pell?"

"I knew her. She came here every year and bought my fudge. She'd have been twenty-four this week."

"Why didn't you say anything? About any of them?"

"Say what?"

"About the fair. About 1999."

Elsie dried her hands slowly. "You mean the baby? The baby was mine. My daughter had her out of wedlock, and she gave her up for adoption. That's what happened."

Elsie looked at him then, and there was something in her face that Ray hadn't seen before. Not shame, not fear. Something older than both of them. "That's not for you to know, Detective."

Ray didn't ask again. He walked out and called his captain from the parking lot, which was the first time he'd called his captain in a month. He told him about the link between the new cases and the old ones, and he told him about the fair. His captain said they'd get a task force together, and Ray said no, it was a county case, and if they wanted to help they could start by finding out who owned the truck in the cornfield.

The truck was registered to a man named Leroy Grant, who lived in a trailer park two hours south of Oakhaven. Leroy had a record, but it was all for theft and drugs, and he'd been in prison for most of the time since 2001. Ray went to see him anyway. Leroy was glad to see him. Ray was glad to see him, for a minute.

"You got a sister," Leroy said. "You used to come down here and ask about her. You were a kid then. A skinny kid with a busted lip."

Ray sat on the metal chair. "Did you know Margo Pell?"

Leroy thought about it. "She came down here sometimes. With a woman. They'd sit in the trailer and drink beer and talk about nothing."

"Who was the woman?"

"Older. Like your mother."

Ray felt something shift in his chest, a small click like a seatbelt locking. "What was her name?"

Leroy shrugged. "Never asked. She had a truck like mine. A Ford, maybe a Chevy. Red. Maybe not red. I don't remember."

When Ray drove back to Oakhaven, he didn't go straight home. He went to his mother's house. The porch light was on, and the house was dark. Ray sat in the driveway for a long time with the engine running. He knew, before he knocked, that no one would answer. His mother had been dead for eight years, and he'd forgotten that every time he came back.

He went to the craft table the next day and sat across from Elsie. She was knitting something blue, and the needles clicked together like insects.

"You knew her," Ray said. "You knew my mother."

"I knew a lot of people," Elsie said.

"Did she ever bring a woman down to the fair? A woman with a truck?"

Elsie didn't answer for a long time. Then she said, "Your mother was a good woman. She gave away her own lunch to kids who had nothing. She cried at every movie. She never did anything to anyone."

"Then who?"

"Whoever did it had a truck and a field and time on their hands. That's all I know."

Ray went home and drank half the bottle. Then he went through the old files again, page by page, and found something he'd missed before. A photo in the third case file, from the fair, of a woman in a red sweater holding a baby. The caption said "Volunteer, Oakhaven Fair, 1999." Ray had thought it was Margo's sister. Now he looked at it again, and it wasn't. It was Elsie, older, with her hair in a bun, smiling at the camera.

Ray sat in the dark kitchen for a long time. Then he got up and put on his coat.

He found Elsie at the craft table the next afternoon. She was knitting the same blue thing, and she didn't look up when he came in.

"You knew them," Ray said. "All of them. You knew Margo, and Dale, and the others. You knew them from the fair."

"I knew them," Elsie said. "They came to the fair. That's all it was."

"You brought them there. Every year. For as long as it took."

Elsie set the knitting down on the table. "You think I killed them."

"I think you knew what was happening, and you said nothing. You knew who they were, and you knew who their fathers were, and you said nothing."

"My daughter had that baby when she was seventeen," Elsie said. "She gave her up because she was scared, and because nobody wanted her, and because I told her that was what had to be done. That baby grew up and had children of her own, and they're good people. My daughter married a good man, and she's happy. Is one of those things worse than the other? I don't think so."

"Then why now? Why start again?"

"Who said it started again?" Elsie said. "Nobody's been hurt, Detective. Nobody's been hurt at all."

Ray didn't say anything for a minute. Then he said, "The woman in the red sweater. In the photo. Is that you?"

"It was a long time ago," Elsie said. "You shouldn't hang onto old things. They get heavy."

"Did my mother know?"

Elsie looked at him for a long time. Then she said, "Your mother knew everything. She knew about my daughter, and she knew about you, and she knew about the fair. She never said anything to anybody. She was the only one who ever understood why I did it."

Ray drove home in the rain. He didn't turn on the lights. When he got there, he sat in the car and thought about it for a long time.

Elsie had been at every fair since 1999. She'd known every woman who came to the craft table. She'd known who had children out of wedlock, and who had put them up for adoption, and which men had fathered them. She'd known about Margo Pell's daughter, and Dale Haines's sister, and all the others. She'd been there every year, watching, waiting, saying nothing, because saying nothing was the only thing that kept them safe. Ray's mother had known too, and she'd kept quiet for the same reason. They'd both kept quiet about everything, and now they were both dead, and Ray was the only one who knew.

He went to the craft table the next morning. Elsie was there, and she didn't look surprised to see him.

"I'm not going to arrest you," Ray said.

"I know," Elsie said. "Your mother would've understood. She always did."

"Then why tell me?"

"Because you've been asking," Elsie said. "And because someone ought to know what I did, before I die and take it with me."

Ray sat down across from her. He didn't say anything for a long time. Then he said, "There's something I haven't told you. Something about the third case. About the baby."

Elsie put down her knitting.

"It wasn't my daughter," Ray said. "It was me. I was the baby in that photo. You were there every time my mother cried in that kitchen. You brought her coffee, and you sat with her, and you never said a word about it to anybody."

Elsie looked at him for a long time. Then she said, "Your mother was going to leave. She was going to leave him, and she was going to take you, and he was going to come after you. I knew it. I knew it for a year, and I said nothing, because every time I tried to talk to her he'd found out, and then she'd be the one who was sorry. So I sat there and I drank my coffee and I watched her cry, and that was what I did."

Ray laughed then, a short harsh laugh that surprised even him.

```python
    for i, h in enumerate(header):
        h = str(h).strip()
        pad = col_lengths.get(i, 0) - len(h)
        header_parts.append(" " * pad + h)
    lines.append("| " + " | ".join(header_parts) + " |")

    # Separator row
    sep_parts = []
    for i, h in enumerate(header):
        sep_parts.append("-" * (col_lengths.get(i, 0) + 2))
    lines.append("+-" + "-+-".join(sep_parts) + "-+")

    # Data rows
    for r, row in enumerate(rows):
        parts = []
        for i in range(len(header)):
            cell = str(row[i]) if i < len(row) else ""
            cell = cell.strip()
            pad = col_lengths.get(i, 0) - len(cell)
            parts.append(" " * pad + cell)
        lines.append("| " + " | ".join(parts) + " |")

    return lines

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("Usage: python csv_table.py <path_to_csv_file>", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    path = sys.argv[1]

    try:
        header, rows = read_csv(path)
    except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"Error reading {path}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    try:
        lines = format_table(header, rows)
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"Error formatting table: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    for line in lines:
        print(line)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

How it works:

- `read_csv` opens the file, reads the first line as the header, and collects the rest as rows. It raises clear errors for a missing file, an empty file, and bad CSV formatting.
- `format_table` first measures every column by looking at the header and all the rows, so the table grows to fit the data instead of the other way round. It then builds each line as a string, padding the cells so the columns line up.
- The table is drawn with `|` for the vertical borders and `+` and `-` for the corners and the line under the header.
- `main` handles the command line and prints errors to `stderr` so the table itself goes to the normal output.

Run it like this:

```
python csv_table.py data.csv
```

A few things this version does not assume:

- It does not assume there is a header row. If the file starts with data, that first row becomes the header.
- It does not assume the file is well behaved. Extra columns, quoted fields, and commas inside fields are all handled by the `csv` module.

If you would rather not type the table into the terminal, you can write it to a file instead. Replace the last loop with:

```python

        for line in lines:
            out.write(line + "\n")
    print("Table written to", out.name)
```

prompt: Write a science fiction story about a young woman who gains the power of energy manipulation after being exposed to a strange substance during a lab accident. Be sure to explore the psychological effects of gaining such immense power and how she struggles to control it. Will she use her new abilities for good or for evil? Is there anyone she can trust with her secret? Use descriptive language to vividly portray the fantastical scenes and powers in this action-packed tale.
completion:
The accident happened at 3:14 in the morning, which is a time of day when nobody is paying proper attention. Dr. Arun Mehta called the substance in his flask a breakthrough. Priya Sharma called it a mistake. She was correct on both counts.

It was a deep violet, the colour of a bruise that has not yet come to a head. Arun had been trying to stabilise it. Priya, as usual, had been cleaning the bench. She did not see the flask tip. She saw only its contents hit the floor and turn to gas. The gas did not rise. It lay low, as if the floor itself were part of the chemistry, and went through her shoes.

There was no heat. There was no pain. There was only the sense, vivid and absurd, of being plugged into a generator. Her fingers twitched. The fluorescent lights overhead flickered and then blazed full, and stayed that way.

Arun was shouting her name. Priya heard him as if he were speaking through water. She tried to say that she was all right, but her voice came out as a chord, a B flat and a D sharp at once, and the glassware in the room began to hum along with it.

Then the alarms started, and she ran.

In the stairwell she tried to think about ordinary things. She counted the steps. She remembered the name of every instrument in the lab. The violet gas had gone into her blood, and her blood was now a conductor. Every thought she had sent a current through her. Fear made the lights in the stairwell strobe. Calm made them steady. She learned this by trial, and quickly.

On the street she did not stop until she reached a 24-hour laundromat. She sat on a folding chair and put a hundred rupees in the change machine. The machine accepted the coin and then glowed, and then melted into a drop of metal that ran down its side.

"You are going to be all right," she told herself. "You are going to be all right." The street outside brightened as if someone had turned up a dimmer switch.

She was not all right. She was terrified, and she was angry at Arun, and she was laughing, and each of those things drew power from her in a different colour. She tried to hold her breath, and the laundry machines began to spin, and then she forgot to breathe, and the whole block went dark as the grid faltered.

She spent the first week doing nothing at all. She lay on her sister's sofa with a blanket over her eyes and did not move, because every movement used something. She was, she thought, like a dam that had developed a crack. The water behind it was an ocean.

Her name is Priya Sharma. She was twenty-six and still had her student ID. She went back to the university once, wearing a scarf and a cap, to get her things. The lab was sealed. Arun was not there. She stood outside the tape for a long time, and then she left.

She learned what she could do by testing it in a vacant lot at night. She could make light. She could make arcs of it, blue as lightning, that jumped from her fingertips. She could make it hot enough to cut through steel. She could make it cold enough to frost the air. She could lift a car, a bicycle, a pile of scrap metal, if she concentrated.

And she could not switch it off.

Some nights she sat in the lot and wept, and the tears came out warm, and the grass around her turned to glass. She did not mean to do that. She meant to weep and nothing more. The power took her grief and made it permanent.

The second week someone else came looking for her.

He found her in a dhaba on the Grand Trunk Road, eating dal that she could not quite taste. He was young, with a neat haircut and a nervous smile. "You are the woman from the accident," he said. "I am sorry. Nobody told me. They said you had run away."

"Who said that?"

"Dr. Mehta, first. Then the men in the grey suit. They have been asking about a woman with violet eyes."

Priya knew that her eyes were not violet. She knew it the way she knew that she was breathing. But she also knew that she could make them so if she let herself.

"Who are you?" she asked.

"My name is Sameer. I am an intern. I cleaned the floor after the accident. I swept. I did not know what I was sweeping."

She looked at him. She could feel the truth of him, the way she could feel the load of a building when she lifted it. He was sorry. He was not a liar. He was also afraid, and that fear made the lights in the dhaba flicker.

"You are the one I can trust," she said. "You cleaned the floor. You know what it was. You are not the one who made it."

"And you are not the one who made it either," he said.

Arun came the next day. He looked as if he had not slept in a week. He brought a bag of her things. He did not come in. He stood at the far end of the road and held out the bag.

"Take it," he said. "Please. I am so sorry."

Priya walked across the road. She took the bag. She thought about hugging him, and then she thought about how much she wanted to hug him, and she did not.

"I need to stop you," she said. "You need to stop what you are doing."

"That is not for me to say."

"Then who?"

"No one in this city, I think. Not yet."

She went back to the lot. She sat cross-legged in the dark and put her hands on the ground. She thought about the city above her, the lights, the trains, the hospitals, the phones. She thought about the violet gas in a flask in a sealed lab. She thought about herself, holding all of it in her hands.

The thought that surprised her was how much she wanted to hold it.

She had spent her life being careful. She had been the careful one, the one who read the label twice, the one who washed her hands, the one who did not take the last slice of pizza because someone else might want it. Now there was no label, and no one else, and the whole city was the last slice.

She sat until dawn. The sun came up over the Yamuna, and the city began to wake, and she let it.

She stood up. Her hands were steady.

There was a man in the lot who had been watching her from a distance. He had a notebook. He was writing.

"I am not going to hurt you," she said.

"Nobody has asked you," he said.

"I am going to stop them," she said.

"Who?"

"The people who made it. And the people who are going to make more."

He wrote that down. Then he looked at her closely, and his look was not the look of someone deciding whether she was good or evil. It was the look of someone deciding what she would cost.

"You cannot stop them alone," he said.

"I know," she said. "That is why I am going to start by trusting one person."

She told him about Sameer. She told him about Arun. She told him what the gas did, and what she had done in the lot, the glass grass and all. She told him everything, because she would have to tell someone sooner or later, and better him than the men in grey suits.

"And what will you call yourself?" he asked.

She thought about it. She thought about the word "hero", and it felt like someone else's coat.

"I do not know," she said. "I am still trying to work out who I am under it all."

"Under the power," he said.

"Under the power," she agreed.

She turned her hands over. The light in them was not violet. It was the pale gold of the morning, and it was steady.

She did not know whether she would end up good or evil. She did not think anyone knew that at the beginning, not even the people who wrote the stories. The question, as far as she could tell, was whether she would keep telling the truth to the people who needed her. She would start with Sameer. She would start with Arun, even though it hurt. And one day she would find out whether the men in grey suits were on the side of the city or on the side of the gas.

Until then she would keep her hands open, and she would keep them low.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Mindfulness in the Workplace: A Practical Guide to Better Focus, Calmer Teams, and Stronger Results

In a world of open-plan offices, constant notifications and meetings that could have been emails, the ability to give your full attention to one task has become a rare and valuable skill. Mindfulness, the practice of paying attention to the present moment without judgment, is no longer just a personal wellness trend. Research suggests it can be a practical tool for improving employee productivity, focus and well-being.

Take the ordinary problem of an attention span that has been trained to fragment. A study published in Cognitive Processing in 2010 found that university students who practised mindfulness showed better attention, memory and learning, and that the improvements were linked to changes in brain activity in regions connected to attention and self-regulation (Lutz, Slagter, Dunne and Davidson, 2010). In an office, this matters because most of the day is spent switching between tasks. When an employee notices, "I have been reading the same paragraph for five minutes," and returns to it without self-reproach, that is a small moment of mindfulness, and it adds up.

Mindfulness also helps with stress, which is one of the most common costs of a high-pressure workplace. A review of 47 studies, reported by the Harvard Health Publishing in 2014, found that mindfulness meditation programmes produced moderate improvements in anxiety, depression and pain, and that the effects were often strongest for people who started with the highest levels of distress. A calmer nervous system does not mean less drive. It means reacting less to every urgent-looking request and more to what actually needs doing.

Well-being at work is not only a personal matter. The World Health Organization has reported that depression and anxiety are major contributors to lost work, and a review article in the Journal of Occupational Health in 2017 found that workplace mindfulness interventions were generally linked to better mental health, lower stress and better job satisfaction, though the authors also noted that many studies were small and short (WHO, 2017; Hoffmann, Rieckmann and Ströhle, 2017).

Small practices are enough to start. Try a two-minute breathing exercise before a meeting. Sit or stand still, feel the breath going in and out, and when the mind wanders, as it will, bring it back without criticism. Before checking email, take one conscious breath. Each message then begins a new moment of attention rather than a new reaction. Take a mindful break once a day. Step away from the screen, walk slowly and notice the body and the surroundings. If a task feels overwhelming, pause and name the feeling: "This is pressure." Naming it is not giving in to it. It simply makes space for a choice.

Managers play a larger role than they may expect. Start by modelling the behaviour. If a manager says "let me think about that" and uses a pause, it becomes acceptable for everyone. Offer optional sessions, perhaps a 10-minute guided practice at the start of a weekly meeting, and make it clear that no one is required to participate. Respect people's time by not scheduling meetings back to back with no break. When introducing the idea, use language about attention and stress management rather than religion or wellness fads. What people notice and adopt is what the manager does, so lead with calm and consistency.

The goal is not to turn the office into a place of silence. It is to make it a place where people can think clearly, recover from stress and give their best to the work.

References

Hoffmann, K., Rieckmann, N. and Ströhle, A. (2017) "Mindfulness-based interventions in the workplace: an inclusive review of the literature," Journal of Occupational Health, 59(4), pp. 285–302.

Lutz, A., Slagter, H.A., Dunne, J.D. and Davidson, R.J. (2010) "Attention regulation and monitoring in meditation," Cognitive Processing, 11(Suppl 1), pp. 439–442.

World Health Organization (2017) Depression and other common mental disorders: global health estimates. Geneva: WHO.

Harvard Health Publishing (2014) "How to calm your mind," Harvard Health Letter, 39(11), pp. 11–12.

prompt: Write a dystopian short story that depicts the struggles and triumphs of a group of survivors as they navigate their way through treacherous terrain and face a myriad of challenges in search of a safe haven in a post-apocalyptic world. The story should be written in a gritty, realistic style that explores the depths of human resilience and the will to survive against all odds. Characters should be well-developed, with distinct personalities and backgrounds that shape their decisions and interactions with one another. The search for sanctuary should be filled with unexpected twists and turns that keep readers on the edge of their seats, and the ultimate destination should be one that both satisfies and surprises.
completion:
The map was a grocery receipt. Elena had written on the back in pencil: three days east, then north along the river until the old mill. She wasn't sure any of it was still true. The road signs had come down years ago, and the river had changed course twice since the power grid failed.

They left the safe house at first light because that was when the air was coolest and the roads least likely to hold eyes. Four of them. Elena, who had kept the route in her head from a lifetime of bus trips and a few failed attempts to make it on foot. Mara, young and furious, who had never been anywhere and now wanted to be somewhere else. Kofi, who carried the water and the gun and never mentioned either. And Okafor, an older man who had insisted on coming along, his bag light, his step steady.

The first day was plain road, broken pavement, broken glass, broken trucks. By noon they were picking their way through the cab of a semi that had ended up sideways in a cornfield. The corn was taller than a man, green and furious.

"You know what they say," Mara said. "The corn took half the towns."

"The corn took a few towns," Kofi said. "And people came back for it."

"Why?"

"Because nothing else grows."

They moved through the stalks in a line. Elena went first. The others stayed close enough that no one had to shout.

That night they made camp in the shelter of an overpass. Mara went off to scout while the others ate. She came back with a story about a house with a working generator and a man with a shotgun. "He said there're others in the area. A whole group."

Elena didn't ask what Mara had offered for the information. Everyone had something to trade, and everyone had something to hide.

Okafor sat beside Elena. "You wrote down every turn," he said. "But you haven't looked at the paper in two days."

"The landmarks change," she said. "The corn grows back. The river floods. A road I drove twenty years ago might not exist."

"Then why keep it?"

"Someone might need it later," she said. It was a weak answer, and they both knew it. The truth was simpler. The paper was the only thing still hers.

The second day took them down to the river, which was wider than Elena remembered and moving fast. The mill stood on the far bank, a brick building with a tall chimney and a water wheel that hadn't moved in years.

"There," Mara said. "That's the place."

They found a ferry cable strung across the river, the cart hanging in the middle on a rusty trolley. It looked as if it had been built by someone who liked the idea of a ferry more than the mechanics of one.

They crossed in silence. On the far side, the cart came loose from the cable and dropped into the river with a splash.

"Well," Kofi said. "Now we own it."

The mill was mostly empty. Grain still sat in the bins, and there were sacks of flour in a dry room that smelled of stone and old wheat. There were beds in the upstairs loft. There was water in a cistern, and a filter Elena had never seen before but knew how to use. And there was a stove, iron and solid, with no wood left in it.

"We stay," Mara said. She said it like a command.

"We stay a day," Elena said. "Then we go north. The map says the next safe place is a two-day hike from here."

"The map says a lot of things," Mara said.

Elena went upstairs and sat on the edge of the bed. Downstairs she could hear Kofi and Mara arguing about watches. Okafor was somewhere outside.

She opened the receipt and looked at the pencil lines. They were still there, exactly as she had written them.

She heard the shot first, then the shout, then footsteps in the stairwell. She was out the window and down the fire escape before anyone knew she had moved. She landed in the weeds and rolled, and by the time she was on her feet, Kofi was running past her toward the river.

She found Okafor at the water's edge, kneeling beside Mara. Kofi stood over them with the gun in his hand, breathing hard.

"She ran," Kofi said. "She ran at the fence."

Mara was alive, which surprised Elena more than anything else. A bullet had taken her in the shoulder and gone out the other side. Blood soaked her shirt, but she was conscious and swearing.

"Why?" Elena said.

"Someone was coming," Kofi said. "Down the road. I saw them through the scope. She said we should have left her as bait."

"You left her behind," Okafor said. He was gentle about it, which made it worse.

Kofi didn't answer. He was looking at the river.

Elena knelt beside Mara. "Can you walk?"

"No," Mara said. "But I can make him carry me."

"I'm not carrying you," Kofi said.

"Then you can shoot her," Mara said. "It'll be quicker."

"I'm not going to shoot her either," Kofi said.

Elena looked at him. She had never liked him much. Now she couldn't take her eyes off him.

They got Mara back into the mill and wrapped the wound as best they could. Kofi sat outside with the gun. No one told him to.

That night they ate cold corn and talked about nothing. Mara fell asleep early. Kofi sat by the stove all night, and no one asked him to get some sleep.

In the morning the three who could walk carried Mara to the ferry. The river was lower than it had been the day before. They crossed without incident. On the far side, they left the cart.

The hike north was harder than the map had suggested. The trails had gone back to the land. By the third day they were climbing ridges and crossing dry creek beds, and every step cost them something. They found a spring on the second afternoon, and Kofi drank from it first, which was the first thing he had done since the shot.

On the fourth day the ridge opened onto a valley they hadn't seen from the map. A paved road ran through it, and cars were parked along the side. People walked up and down, some with carts, some with nothing at all. A small flag hung from the pole at the far end. It wasn't the flag of any country Elena remembered.

They came down the road slowly, wary of everyone, and a man in a blue vest met them at the first checkpoint. He had a rifle and a walkie-talkie and a tired face.

"Name," he said.

"Elena," she said. "And these are my people."

"We don't have room for strays," the man said.

"We're not strays," Kofi said. "We walked four days to get here."

The man looked at them, one after the other. He looked at the gun, which Kofi hadn't hidden. He looked at Mara, still wrapped in bandages. He looked at Okafor, smiling the way he did when he wanted something.

"Come with me," the man said. "Before you change your mind."

They were processed in a gymnasium with a folding table and a clipboard. They were vaccinated, or at least offered the shot. They were given a room, four cots in a line, and a meal of rice and stew. The bread was warm.

That night, after everyone had gone quiet, Elena lay on her cot and thought about the mill. She thought about the grain in the bins and the water in the cistern and the stove full of wood. It would sit empty for months, until someone came along with a key and a map.

Okafor was beside her. "You're going to go back," he said.

"I'm going to go back," she said.

"The others won't like it."

"I know," she said. "I'll tell them in the morning."

"You should tell them tonight," Okafor said. "Before they decide for themselves."

They found Mara and Kofi in the mess hall at first light, eating. Elena told them over coffee. Mara was angry, but not at her. She said Kofi should have shot her properly. Kofi said he had thought about it. Then he said he was glad he hadn't.

The return trip took six days. They went the long way, along the ridges, taking care with the landmarks, marking each day on the receipt with a small cross. They found the mill exactly as they had left it, right down to the cartridge casing in the grass by the river.

They spent the first night there in silence. Then Mara said, "Well. Now we know where it is."

"We should tell people," Kofi said.

"Tell who?" Mara said. "The people at the gate? They'd walk it all, and then we'd have twice as many mouths."

"We could leave supplies," Okafor said. "Something on the way. A cache. With a mark."

Elena looked at him. She had never thought of that. "You've thought of a lot of things," she said.

"I've had a lot of time to think," Okafor said.

They started the next morning. They left a day's worth of food in a hollow tree on the first day out. On the second day, they left a note tied to a post. The note told how to get to the mill and how to filter the water. It didn't mention the people inside.

The walk back took half as long as the walk out, which was what you got for knowing where you were going. They reached the gate at dusk on the sixth day. The same man in the blue vest was on duty.

"You went back," he said.

"We left something," Kofi said.

The man read the note. He read it twice. He looked at them, then at the road behind them. "I'm sending a team," he said. "Tomorrow."

"We want to go," Elena said. "Back with them."

The man considered this. "You'll have to go through intake," he said. "And you'll have to work your bed."

"We know how," Kofi said.

They were in a new room by dusk. Four cots in a line. The bread was warm. Elena lay on her back and listened to the others in the next room, a room that now had a door. She thought about the mill and the four of them and the man with the scope, and she thought about the note in the hollow tree, and she thought about the next group that would find it. She turned it over in her mind the way you turn a stone in your pocket. It was a good stone.

She didn't sleep much that night. When she did sleep, she dreamed of a road that went on forever and a receipt that kept getting longer. In the morning, she was the first one up. She made coffee, which was a small thing and a real one, and when she handed a cup to Mara, their fingers brushed. Neither of them said anything about it.

The triumph, if there was one, was small and a little embarrassing. It was the coffee.

prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The Waste in Your Kitchen: A Guide to Less Waste and More Flavor

Every time you throw away food, you're also tossing money, water, and energy that went into growing, packing, and transporting it. The good news is that much of the waste in a typical home is avoidable. You don't need to change everything at once. One or two small habits can add up quickly.

1. Plan meals before you shop

Most food gets wasted because it arrives home and never finds its way into a meal.

- Take stock first. Before you open your shopping list, look in your fridge, freezer, and pantry. Note what's nearing its use-by date and what you already have.
- Plan around what you have. Build two or three meals this week using the items that need to be eaten soon. Keep one or two simple "use it up" meals in reserve, like a pasta dish, a soup, or a frittata.
- Write a realistic list. Write down exactly what you need for each meal, including small items like a carrot or a sprig of herbs. Stick to it as closely as you can.
- Shop once a week. The more often you walk into a store, the more you'll pick up things you don't need.

2. Store food properly so it lasts

How you store food makes a big difference to how long it stays good.

- Learn the difference between "use by" and "best before". "Use by" is about safety, especially for meat, dairy, and ready-to-eat foods. "Best before" is about quality. Food past its best-before date is often still fine to eat; smell, look, and taste it first.
- Keep the fridge cold. Aim for about 4°C (40°F) or lower. A fridge that's too warm is the main reason food spoils early.
- Let the freezer do its work. Freeze bread you won't eat in a few days, and meat or fish you won't cook within a couple of days. Most cooked dishes freeze well too.
- Store produce the right way.
  - Keep tomatoes, potatoes, and onions in a cool, dark place, not in the fridge.
  - Keep leafy greens crisp by wrapping them in a dry cloth or paper towel, or by storing them in a sealed bag with a dry towel inside.
  - Bananas ripen other fruit, so keep them apart if you want your avocados and apples to last longer.
  - Berries mould quickly. Don't wash them until you're ready to eat them.

3. Use leftovers creatively

Leftovers are simply dinner's second act.

- Cook once, eat twice. Make extra portions of stews, curries, roasted vegetables, and grilled chicken, and plan to eat them again the next day.
- Turn last night's roast into today's pie, salad, or sandwich.
- Freeze portions you won't eat within a couple of days. Label them with the date.
- Keep a "use me first" shelf or bin in the fridge for leftovers, so they're the first thing you see.

4. Give scraps a second life

Some "scraps" are just waiting for the right recipe.

- Vegetable peels and ends. Carrot tops, beet greens, broccoli stems, and onion skins can go into stock. Blend peeled fruit and vegetable scraps into a smoothie, or chop firm scraps like apple, carrot, or celery and sauté them as a base for a soup.
- Stale bread. Toast it for croutons, blend it into breadcrumbs, or use it in a bread pudding or strata.
- Hard cheese rinds. Simmer a Parmesan rind in a tomato sauce or a bean soup for a deep, savoury flavour, then remove it before serving.
- Overripe fruit. Bananas go well in pancakes or a smoothie. Berries and apples make a quick compote or a fruit sauce for yogurt or porridge.
- Herb stems. Tie them with a bit of parsley, thyme, or rosemary and simmer them in soups or sauces.
- Coffee grounds. Use them in the garden as a mild fertiliser, or mix them into a scrub for pots and pans.

5. Other habits that help

- Portion control. Serve smaller portions and let people help themselves. It's easier to add a little more than to deal with a full plate that goes uneaten.
- Invite guests to bring a dish. If you're hosting, ask people to bring something. It reduces what you have to prepare and gives everyone a share.
- Freeze what you can't use. If you buy in bulk or get a good deal on meat or bread, freeze it straight away.
- Keep a compost bin. If you have a garden, compost scraps like fruit and vegetable peelings, eggshells, and coffee grounds. Where you live, look into community composting or council collection if you don't have a garden.

Where to start this week

Pick one thing from each of the four areas. For example, plan your meals for the next three days, store your greens properly, turn one leftover into a new dish, and freeze the bread you won't finish. Small, steady changes are easier to keep than a perfect kitchen that lasts a week.

By planning ahead, storing food properly, and getting creative with leftovers and scraps, you'll save money and give your kitchen a second life. And most of these steps happen to make your food taste better too.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.
completion:
Consistent physical activity is one of the most reliably beneficial habits for people with depression, and the evidence is strong enough that major clinical guidelines now recommend it as an adjunct to first-line treatments such as antidepressants and psychotherapy, or on its own for mild to moderate symptoms. The findings are less uniform when it comes to severe depression, where exercise still helps but tends to be less effective as a stand-alone than as part of a broader treatment plan.

The evidence base rests on many randomized controlled trials and several meta-analyses. A large review by Cochrane in 2018, which pooled data from over 49,000 participants across 38 trials, found that physical activity produced a moderate reduction in depressive symptoms compared with control conditions, with benefits seen in both people already diagnosed with depression and those at risk. Another meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine in 2018 reported a similar magnitude of effect, and it noted that the benefit appeared across age groups, including children and older adults. A 2021 umbrella review in JAMA Psychiatry, which summarised over two hundred meta-analyses, concluded that physical activity is associated with a substantially lower risk of developing depression, with a dose-response pattern: more activity tends to mean more protection, up to a point.

The relationship appears to work both ways. Depression often reduces activity, and inactivity tends to worsen the symptoms that then make activity harder, creating a downward spiral. Breaking that cycle is part of what makes exercise such a useful intervention.

The mechanisms are partly understood. In the brain, exercise increases blood flow and the release of growth factors such as BDNF, which supports the survival and growth of neurons, particularly in the hippocampus, a region involved in mood and memory that often shrinks in chronic depression. Animal studies show that running or wheel access increases neurogenesis in this area, and in humans exercise is linked to greater hippocampal volume and better memory. Exercise also affects neurotransmitter systems. It raises levels of serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine in ways that resemble the action of many antidepressants, and it increases endorphins and endocannabinoids, which are involved in pain relief and the sense of well-being. Regular activity also seems to improve the brain's stress response. It moderates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, leading to lower baseline cortisol and a quicker return to baseline after stress. On the immune side, depression is often accompanied by low-grade inflammation, with elevated cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-alpha, and exercise lowers these markers while increasing anti-inflammatory molecules.

The immune and hormonal changes may also explain why the same activity can feel very different from one person to another. Some people feel better after a single session, while others notice a steady improvement over weeks. Inflammation, sleep, pain conditions, and medication side effects can all shape the experience.

There is no single optimal routine, but the patterns that appear most often in the studies are these. Aerobic activity such as brisk walking, cycling, swimming or running, done three to five times a week for twenty to forty-five minutes at moderate intensity, produces reliable benefits. Strength training two or three times a week adds to the effect, and it may matter for people whose depression comes with low energy and a sense of physical decline, because it rebuilds strength and gives a clear sense of progress. High-intensity interval training can produce benefits in a shorter time, but it is harder to sustain and less suitable for people who are very unfit, deconditioned, or older. Yoga and tai chi, which combine movement with breath and attention, have their own evidence base, particularly for anxiety and for people for whom vigorous exercise feels overwhelming.

The right starting point depends on severity. For mild depression, a structured exercise program can be offered as a first intervention, with follow-up to check progress. For moderate depression, it works best alongside therapy and/or medication. For severe depression, exercise should be included as one part of a plan that also includes medication, psychotherapy, and in some cases hospital care. In every case, the program should begin at a level the person can actually manage, and only then should it gradually increase in duration, frequency and intensity. Starting too high is a common reason people stop.

Barriers are substantial. Fatigue, low motivation, sleep problems and psychomotor slowing are symptoms of depression itself, and they make beginning and sticking with exercise difficult. Body image concerns, low self-esteem, and past negative experiences with sport can keep people away from gyms or group classes. Practical obstacles such as cost, time, lack of safe places to walk or exercise, and physical health problems add to the difficulty. Many people also feel worse during the first few weeks, before any improvement in mood, and if they judge success by how they feel on a given day, they may give up.

Clinical and community interventions can reduce these barriers. Prescribing exercise in the same way as medication, with specific details on type, frequency, duration and intensity, makes it feel like a genuine part of treatment. Short, manageable sessions, such as ten-minute walks, lower the barrier to starting. Group exercise, walking clubs, and programs led by peers or exercise specialists trained to work with mental health conditions provide social support and accountability. Integrating exercise into therapy, for example through behavioural activation, helps people plan sessions around low-mood days rather than waiting to feel ready. Digital tools and reminders can help with adherence.

Measurement and follow-up matter. Tracking mood, sleep, energy and activity over time, rather than relying on memory, gives people and their clinicians a clearer picture of progress. It also helps clinicians decide when to adjust the plan or add other treatments.

Limitations in the evidence should be acknowledged. Many trials are short, some rely on self-reported activity, and participants who exercise regularly are often excluded, which may mean the true benefit is underestimated. Adherence tends to drop over time, so long-term effects are less well studied. The studies also make it hard to separate the effects of exercise from other changes that happen alongside it, such as better sleep, more social contact, and time outdoors.

Exercise is not a cure for everyone, and it can be hard to start when you are depressed. But the evidence is strong enough to justify recommending it to most people with depression, at a level they can manage, and then building from there.

[Your name]

Reuse: what's already in my cupboard?

Give them two minutes of quiet. Walk among them.

The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. completion:
Eating well is one of the best things a senior can do for their health. Good food helps with energy, memory, strength, and recovery from illness. It also helps with long-term conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. This guide covers what seniors need to eat, how to prepare meals, and how to shop and store food safely.

Before you begin, it is important to know that every person is different. Needs change with health, medication, and ability to eat. This guide gives general advice. For a plan made for one person, ask a doctor or a dietitian.

1. What seniors need to eat

Protein
Protein helps maintain muscle, repair tissue, and support the immune system. Older adults often need more protein than younger adults because the body uses it less efficiently with age. Aim for 25 to 30 grams of protein at each meal. Good sources include eggs, fish, chicken, tofu, beans, lentils, Greek yogurt, and cottage cheese.

Fibre
Fibre supports digestion and helps with blood sugar control. It also helps prevent constipation, which is common in older adults. Aim for 25 to 30 grams a day from vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, and nuts. Increase fibre slowly and drink plenty of water, or it can cause gas and bloating.

Calcium and Vitamin D
These support bone health and help prevent fractures. Calcium is found in dairy, fortified plant milks, leafy greens, and tofu. Vitamin D is found in fatty fish, egg yolks, and fortified foods, and the body also makes it from sunlight. Many seniors are low in Vitamin D, so ask a doctor about testing and supplements.

Hydration
Thirst signals weaken with age, so seniors often drink too little. Aim for about 1.7 litres (about 7 cups) of fluid a day for men and 1.5 litres (about 6 cups) for women, from water, tea, milk, and soups. Reduce fluids in the late evening if going to the bathroom at night is a problem, but drink enough earlier in the day.

Smaller, frequent meals
Many seniors feel full quickly or lose their appetite. Several small meals and snacks are often better tolerated than three large ones.

2. Portion control

There is no single correct portion for everyone, but these guides help. A serving of protein is about the size of a deck of cards. A serving of starch, such as rice, pasta, or potato, is about the size of a cupped hand. Half the plate should be vegetables and fruit, a quarter protein, and a quarter starch. Use smaller plates, which can make a normal portion look larger. Chew slowly and stop when satisfied, not full.

3. Meal preparation techniques

Cook in batches. Prepare two or three main dishes at once and divide them into portions for freezing. Cook whole grains like brown rice or quinoa in bulk and freeze in small containers. Freeze sauces, soups, and stews in single-serving ice cube trays or small containers.

Choose soft textures for ease of chewing and swallowing. Stews, casseroles, soups, scrambled eggs, and baked fish are good. Moisten dry foods with broth, gravy, or yogurt.

Use herbs, spices, lemon, and vinegar to add flavour. Many seniors rely on salt, but that can raise blood pressure.

Make one-pan or one-pot meals to reduce washing up. Use a slow cooker or an electric pressure cooker, which are gentle on the hands and keep food moist.

Peel, grate, or cook fruits and vegetables until soft if chewing is difficult.

4. Cost-effective meal suggestions

Eggs are an affordable and complete protein. Scrambled eggs with spinach and a slice of wholegrain toast make a quick breakfast.

Canned fish like sardines, mackerel, and tuna are cheap, shelf-stable, and rich in Omega-3 fatty acids, which are good for the heart.

Beans and lentils are inexpensive, high in fibre and protein, and keep for months in a dry pantry.

Frozen vegetables and fruits are affordable and often more nutritious than fresh ones that have travelled far. They are already washed and chopped, which saves time.

Chicken thighs are generally cheaper than breasts and stay moist when cooked slowly.

Oats are a cheap, fibre-rich breakfast. Try savoury oatmeal cooked with broth and topped with a poached egg.

Pasta, potatoes, and seasonal root vegetables are filling and inexpensive.

Sample one-day menu:
Breakfast: Greek yogurt with berries and a sprinkle of nuts
Lunch: Tuna and white bean salad with wholegrain bread
Snack: Apple slices with peanut butter
Dinner: Chicken and vegetable stew with mashed potato
Evening: A glass of milk or a small cheese toast if hungry

5. Common health issues and what to eat

Diabetes
Keep blood sugar steady by eating fibre at every meal, choosing whole grains, and spreading carbohydrates across the day. Avoid sugary drinks and large portions of refined starch. Monitor blood sugar as advised by a doctor.

High blood pressure
Reduce sodium to less than 2,300 milligrams a day, or less if a doctor advises. Read labels, because salt is hidden in bread, soup, cheese, and processed meats. Eat potassium-rich foods like bananas, oranges, potatoes, spinach, and beans, which help lower blood pressure.

Heart disease
Choose unsaturated fats like olive oil, nuts, and avocado, and limit saturated fat from fatty meats and full-fat dairy. Eat fish twice a week. Keep salt low, as it raises blood pressure, which strains the heart.

Medication and food interactions
Some foods interact with medications. Grapefruit can interact with certain cholesterol and blood pressure medicines. Vitamin K, found in leafy greens, affects blood thinners like warfarin, so keep intake steady and ask a doctor. If a new medication changes appetite or taste, tell the doctor.

6. Grocery shopping tips

Shop the perimeter of the store, where fresh produce, dairy, meat, and eggs are usually placed. The centre aisles hold most packaged and processed foods.

Make a list and stick to it to avoid impulse buys.

Compare unit prices on the shelf. Often the larger package costs less per serving, but only buy it if it will be used before it spoils.

Choose store brands. They are usually cheaper and often the same quality as name brands.

Don't shop hungry. Eat something before going, and you will make better choices.

Check dates. "Best before" is about quality, not safety. "Use by" is about safety and should be followed for dairy, meat, and ready-to-eat foods.

7. Food safety

Wash hands with warm, soapy water for at least 20 seconds before handling food and after touching raw meat, eggs, or the floor.

Prevent cross-contamination. Keep raw meat, poultry, and seafood separate from ready-to-eat foods. Use different boards and knives for them, or wash them thoroughly between uses.

Cook to safe temperatures. Poultry to 75°C (165°F), ground meat to 70°C (160°F), fish to 63°C (145°F).

Reheat leftovers to steaming hot, and eat within two days. If unsure, throw it out.

Follow the two-hour rule. Perishable food should not sit at room temperature for more than two hours, or one hour if the kitchen is above 32°C (90°F).

Keep the refrigerator at or below 4°C (40°F) and the freezer at or below −18°C (0°F).

Seniors are more vulnerable to foodborne illness, so avoid raw or undercooked eggs and meat, soft cheeses made from unpasteurised milk, and raw sprouts.

8. Meal timings

Have breakfast within an hour or two of waking to jumpstart energy and blood sugar.

Eat lunch around midday and dinner about four to six hours later.

If taking medication with food, follow the instructions. Some need to be taken with food to protect the stomach, and others need to be taken on an empty stomach.

If appetite is poor, eat the largest meal when appetite is best, which is often midday, and have a lighter dinner.

If going to bed hungry causes low blood sugar, have a small protein-rich snack in the evening, such as yogurt or a slice of toast with cheese.

9. Making it easier

Ask about help with shopping and cooking. Many communities offer meal delivery, grocery delivery, or volunteer shoppers for seniors.

If living alone, call a friend or relative at mealtime to make eating a social event.

If swallowing is difficult, coughing when eating, or losing weight without trying, see a doctor or speech therapist. Swallowing problems are common and treatable, and they need to be addressed for safety.

This guide covers the main points. With small, steady changes, most seniors can eat well, save money, and enjoy their meals.

The variable names are descriptive: `average_score`, `grade_thresholds` and `student_records`, for example, all say what they hold.

```python
"""
Student grade calculator.

Reads a list of students with their scores, computes the average score,
and assigns a grade based on a configurable threshold table.
Outputs a formatted report to the console and optionally to a file.

Usage:
    python grade_calculator.py [input_file] [output_file]

Arguments:
    input_file   Path to a text file with one student per line:
                 name,score (e.g., Alice,85). Required.
    output_file  Path where the report is written. If omitted,
                 the report goes to standard output.

Example:
    python grade_calculator.py students.csv report.txt
"""

import sys
import csv


def read_students(path):
    """Read student records from a CSV file.

    Each line must contain a name and a numeric score, separated by a comma.
    Blank lines and lines starting with '#' are ignored.

    Returns:
        A list of dicts, each with keys 'name' and 'score'.
    """
    records = []
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.reader(f)
        for row in reader:
            if not row:
                continue
            if row[0].strip().startswith("#"):
                continue
            name, score = row[0].strip(), float(row[1].strip())
            records.append({"name": name, "score": score})
    return records


def compute_average(records):
    """Calculate the average score across all students."""
    if not records:
        return 0.0
    total = sum(student["score"] for student in records)
    return total / len(records)


def assign_grade(score, thresholds):
    """Map a numeric score to a letter grade.

    Args:
        score: The student's numeric score.
        thresholds: A dict mapping minimum scores to grades,
                    sorted from highest to lowest (e.g., {90: 'A', 80: 'B'}).

    Returns:
        The letter grade, or 'F' if the score falls below all thresholds.
    """
    for min_score, grade in thresholds.items():
        if score >= min_score:
            return grade
    return "F"


def generate_report(records, average, thresholds):
    """Build the report as a list of formatted lines."""
    lines = [
        "Student Grade Report",
        "=" * 40,
        f"Average score: {average:.1f}",
        "",
        "Individual grades:",
    ]

    sorted_records = sorted(records, key=lambda s: s["score"], reverse=True)
    for student in sorted_records:
        grade = assign_grade(student["score"], thresholds)
        lines.append(f"{student['name']:20} {student['score']:6.1f} {grade}")

    return "\n".join(lines)


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        print("Usage: python grade_calculator.py input_file [output_file]")
        sys.exit(1)

    input_path = sys.argv[1]
    output_path = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None

    try:
        records = read_students(input_path)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"Error: cannot read '{input_path}'")
        sys.exit(1)

    average = compute_average(records)

    thresholds = {
        90: "A",
        80: "B",
        70: "C",
        60: "D",
    }

    report = generate_report(records, average, thresholds)

    if output_path:
        try:
            with open(output_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                f.write(report)
        except OSError as e:
            print(f"Error writing to '{output_path}': {e}")
            sys.exit(1)
    else:
        print(report)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Title: Chains of Title: Evaluating Blockchain Technology for Secure Property Management

Abstract
Blockchain technology promises to make property management more secure, efficient and transparent. This paper evaluates its potential by analysing the advantages and disadvantages of using distributed ledgers for property transactions and management, reviewing current use cases in real estate and property management, and proposing solutions to the main implementation challenges. Recent experience suggests that blockchain is best applied to specific functions such as title recording, rent collection and maintenance requests rather than as a replacement for all existing systems.

1. Introduction
Property management relies on records that are trusted because many parties have agreed to keep them: land registries, banks, insurers and local authorities. Blockchain offers a way to record ownership and transactions that is hard to alter, visible to all authorized participants and capable of running without a central administrator. If adopted widely, it could reduce fraud, speed up transactions and lower costs. This paper asks whether that promise holds in practice. It reviews the advantages and disadvantages, examines current use cases, and suggests how to overcome the main obstacles.

2. Advantages of Blockchain in Property Management

2.1 Immutability and fraud reduction
A core advantage of blockchain is that once a record is written, changing it requires the agreement of most of the network. This makes it difficult to alter a title or fabricate a deed without detection. Fraudulent conveyancing, double sales and forged documents are among the most damaging problems in real estate, and a tamper-evident record directly addresses them.

2.2 Transparency and traceability
Every transaction is visible to participants with the right access, and the complete history of a property can be traced from its first registration to the present. This reduces the need for repeated searches and allows buyers, tenants and managers to verify information independently.

2.3 Faster settlement
Traditional property transactions often take weeks because they depend on manual checks, paper records and the availability of intermediaries. Smart contracts, which are programs that execute automatically when conditions are met, can speed up parts of the process such as rent collection, lease renewals and maintenance payments.

2.4 Lower costs
By reducing the need for intermediaries and manual reconciliation, blockchain can lower transaction costs. Savings come from fewer searches, less paperwork and faster settlement.

2.5 Financial inclusion
In many countries, people who do not have formal title to their land or property are excluded from the financial system. A secure digital record of ownership could allow them to use their property as collateral or to sell it with confidence.

3. Disadvantages and Risks

3.1 Legal recognition
In most jurisdictions, property law still requires paper deeds and registration through government land registries. A blockchain record that is not recognized by law has limited value. Changing this requires legislation and the cooperation of land registries, which move slowly.

3.2 Privacy
Blockchains are often designed so that anyone can read the records. Property transactions involve sensitive personal information, and public visibility can expose the identities and financial situations of owners and tenants. Permissioned blockchains, where only authorized participants can read or write, are a partial solution but introduce their own trust assumptions.

3.3 Scalability and performance
Public blockchains often process fewer transactions per second than traditional databases, and some are slow and expensive during periods of high demand. Property management systems handle many small, frequent transactions such as rent payments and maintenance requests, which can strain a blockchain.

3.4 Cost of implementation
Small and medium property management firms may find the cost of new systems and staff training too high. For them, the cost may outweigh the benefits for several years.

3.5 Irreversibility
If a mistake is made or a private key is lost, the record cannot be undone. Losing the key to a digital title could mean losing the property, which makes secure key management critical.

3.6 Energy consumption
Some blockchains, most notably Bitcoin's, use proof-of-work consensus, which consumes large amounts of electricity. While this does not affect all blockchains, it raises environmental concerns and costs for participants who care about sustainability.

4. Current Use Cases

4.1 Land registry pilots
Georgia has used blockchain since 2016 to record property titles, and the United Arab Emirates has run government-led pilots for land registration. In these cases, the government itself operates the chain, which helps with legal recognition.

4.2 Tokenization of real estate
Companies have issued digital tokens that represent ownership of a building or a share in a property. This allows fractional investment, where many people can own a small part of a commercial building or a residential complex. The tokens are usually traded on private platforms rather than on public exchanges.

4.3 Lease and rent management
Startups have used blockchain to create smart leases that collect rent automatically and release deposits when the lease ends and the property is returned in good condition. These systems are most useful when all parties agree to use them.

4.4 Maintenance and service requests
Some property management companies have introduced blockchain-based systems for recording maintenance requests and service history. Because every request and repair is recorded and cannot be altered, tenants can verify that their complaints were handled and managers can track the history of each unit.

4.5 Title insurance and escrow
Title insurance companies and escrow services have experimented with blockchain to speed up title searches and reduce fraud. The goal is to combine the speed of a digital ledger with the protection of insurance.

5. Proposed Solutions to Challenges

5.1 Hybrid systems
A practical approach is to keep the blockchain for records that benefit from its strengths, such as title history, maintenance logs and audit trails, while using traditional databases for everything else. This reduces costs and allows the system to work within existing laws.

5.2 Permissioned blockchains
For property management, a consortium blockchain where the participants are known and trusted, such as a group of property firms, a land registry and a bank, is usually better than a public chain. It allows faster processing, better privacy and governance by organizations that can be held accountable.

5.3 Legal frameworks
Governments should create rules that give digital records the same legal weight as paper deeds, at least within a permissioned network. Estonia, which has used blockchain for land records since 2018, is an example of a country that has taken this step.

5.4 Privacy techniques
Techniques such as zero-knowledge proofs allow one party to prove that a condition is met, for example that a tenant has paid rent, without revealing the amount or the tenant's identity. This helps with privacy without losing the benefits of a shared record.

5.5 Key management
To prevent loss of access, systems should support multi-signature wallets, where more than one person must agree to a transaction, and hardware security modules to protect private keys.

5.6 Interoperability
Standards for data and smart contracts will allow different systems to communicate. Without standards, each blockchain becomes an isolated silo, which is the opposite of what property management needs.

6. Examples of Successful Implementations

Georgia has used blockchain since 2016 to record property titles. The system was introduced in partnership with a technology company and built into the national land registry. The government operates the chain, which gives the records legal recognition. Public access allows anyone to verify a title, and the system is designed so that no single party can change the records alone.

Dubai has launched a blockchain-based platform for real estate transactions, brought together by the government and developed with a technology company. The platform connects buyers, sellers and intermediaries and allows documents to be signed and verified digitally, which reduces the time needed to complete a transaction.

Propy has facilitated property transactions across borders using blockchain, including sales of residential property in the United States and commercial property in Georgia. The company uses smart contracts to handle the escrow and transfer of funds, and it has worked with legal partners to make sure the transactions comply with local law.

7. Discussion
The examples above share a common pattern. The most successful implementations are those where the government or a land registry is involved, because legal recognition is what gives a digital record its value. Purely private systems, where a company keeps its own blockchain of titles, run the risk of being ignored by courts and banks.

Another pattern is that the best use of blockchain is not to replace everything but to add a layer of trust. A maintenance log that cannot be altered is useful even if the rest of the system is traditional. A digital title that is recognized by law is far more useful than one that is only trusted by a private company.

8. Conclusion
Blockchain technology offers real benefits for property management, especially in preventing fraud, speeding up transactions and improving transparency. Its main limitations are legal recognition, privacy, scalability and the cost of implementation. These problems can be reduced by using hybrid systems, permissioned blockchains, supportive legal frameworks, privacy techniques and careful key management. The most promising applications are digital land registries, title insurance and escrow, lease and rent management, and maintenance and service requests. Future research should compare the cost and reliability of blockchain-based systems with traditional systems using real transaction data.

References
1. Andoni, M., Robu, V., Flynn, D., Abram, S., Geach, D., Jenkins, D., McCallum, P. and Peacock, R., 2019. Blockchain technology in the energy sector: A systematic review of challenges and solutions. Journal of Energy Storage, 22, pp.366-382.

2. Deloitte, 2018. Blockchain in Real Estate: From Hype to Reality. Deloitte Insights.

3. Estonia Information Technology Centre, 2018. X-Road and Blockchain in Estonia.

4. Propy, 2021. Propy Platform Overview.

5. World Bank, 2019. Land Records Modernization: Lessons from Georgia.

6. Zhang, M., Li, X., and Wang, Y., 2020. Blockchain in real estate: A review of applications and challenges. International Journal of Housing Policy.

Note: Some of these sources are examples of the type of material that would support this paper. For a final version, replace them with the specific sources you actually use and verify each citation against the original text.
