prompt: Develop a comprehensive social media strategy to promote a new line of eco-friendly home accessories with a focus on brand awareness, engagement, and conversion. The strategy should include identifying target audience demographics, creating a content calendar with a mix of product features, educational posts on eco-friendliness, and user-generated content. Also, include a plan to collaborate with influencers and eco-friendly lifestyle bloggers to reach a wider audience. The style of posts should be visually appealing, using high-quality images and videos showcasing the products in a home setting. Finally, the strategy should outline the key performance indicators to track the success of the campaign, such as engagement rates, referral traffic, and sales conversion rates.
completion:
Here's a complete plan you can hand to a social media manager and start using within a week.

1. Audience

Primary audience
- Age 25 to 40, mostly women, living in cities and suburbs.
- Renters and first-time homeowners who want to make their place feel good without big renovations.
- Interested in sustainable living, minimalism, interior design, and mindful consumption.
- Active on Instagram, Pinterest, TikTok and Facebook.
- Willing to pay a little more for items that look good and last.

Secondary audience
- Couples setting up their first home together.
- Gift buyers looking for eco-conscious presents.
- Home office workers who spend all day at their desk.

Personas
- May, 31, renter: "I want my apartment to feel warm and put-together, but I can't paint or replace fixtures. I also try to avoid single-use plastics."
- Priya and Dev, 29 and 33, first-time homeowners: "We're on a budget and overwhelmed by choices. We want things that look good and don't come with a guilt trip."
- Tom, 38, remote worker: "I spend 8 hours a day at my desk. I want accessories that are nice to look at and good for me."

2. Brand position and voice

Positioning
- Accessories that make an ordinary home feel considered, one small swap at a time.
- Every piece does three things: it looks good, it lasts, and it leaves less behind.

Voice
- Warm, honest and never preachy.
- Short captions that show, not tell.
- Always answer the question "why does this matter?" in one sentence or less.

3. Content pillars

Product features
- Show the product in a real home: on a kitchen counter, beside a bed, on a desk.
- Short videos of the product in use: pouring from a jug, wiping a surface, arranging a shelf.
- Details that matter: materials, size, what it replaces.
- Before and after: a cluttered corner versus the same corner with the product.

Eco-education
- What each material is and where it comes from: bamboo, recycled glass, ceramic, natural fibres, wood.
- Why it matters: durability, what happens at the end of its life, how it compares to the plastic version.
- Care and repair: how to clean it, how to make it last.
- Myths: "eco-friendly" doesn't always mean "biodegradable", and "natural" doesn't always mean "better".

User-generated content
- Customer photos and videos of their homes.
- Before and after swaps.
- Questions that invite answers: "Which corner needs a refresh: kitchen, bathroom or desk?"
- Repost with permission and credit the creator.

Behind the scenes
- Packing orders, the design process, sourcing decisions.
- The team and their own homes.
- Honest posts about packaging and shipping.

4. Content calendar

Weekly rhythm
- 4 to 5 feed posts per week.
- 3 to 5 Stories per week.
- 1 long-form post or reel per week.
- 1 community post per week: questions, polls, "this or that".

Sample 2-week calendar

Week 1
- Monday: Product feature. Ceramic jug on a kitchen counter. Caption: "The 2026 jug, now in matte sage. Keeps water cold for hours. Hand-thrown, built to last decades."
- Tuesday: Eco-education. "Plastic vs. ceramic: what's the difference?" Short reel.
- Wednesday: User-generated. Customer photo of a bathroom shelf. Repost with permission.
- Thursday: Product feature. Desk organiser in natural wood. Video of it being filled.
- Friday: Behind the scenes. Packing an order, with a note about recyclable packaging.
- Sunday: Community post. Poll: "Which room should we feature next?"

Week 2
- Monday: Eco-education. "What does 'biodegradable' actually mean?" Carousel.
- Tuesday: Product feature. Throw blanket in organic cotton. Flat lay with a book and a cup.
- Wednesday: User-generated. "Show us your swap." Call to action to post a before and after and tag the brand.
- Thursday: Product feature. Reusable food wraps. Short tutorial reel.
- Friday: Testimonial. A review from a customer, displayed over a photo of their home.
- Sunday: Community post. "Ask us anything about materials."

Visual style
- Natural light, real homes, no sterile studio shots.
- Warm neutrals with one or two accent colours per post.
- Consistent fonts and a simple logo lockup on every image.
- Vertical video for Reels, TikTok and Stories.

5. Influencer and blogger plan

Who to work with
- Eco-friendly lifestyle bloggers: readers who trust their judgement on sustainable living.
- Home and interior creators: people whose followers come for the room makeovers.
- Micro-influencers (5,000 to 50,000 followers): higher engagement, lower cost, more believable.
- Local makers and shop owners: ceramicists, woodworkers, zero-waste shop owners.

Selection criteria
- Real engagement: comments that look like real people, not bots.
- Aesthetic that fits: warm, home-focused, honest.
- Past work with home or sustainability brands, and how well it performed.
- Audience matches your personas.

Offer
- Free products for honest reviews.
- Affiliate code: 15% off for their followers, 10% commission on sales.
- Paid partnerships for larger creators, clearly marked as sponsored.
- Exclusive launch discount for their audience.

Outreach
- Personalised email or DM. "We love your post about [specific thing]. Our [product] fits with it because [reason]."
- Provide a media kit: product photos, key facts, sustainability notes, pricing.
- Clear brief: what you want, what's required, timeline, disclosure rules.

Sample outreach email
"Hi [name], I'm [your name] from [brand]. We make [product] for people who want their home to feel good without the waste. Your post on [topic] really hit home with us. Would you be open to trying a piece and sharing your honest thoughts? Happy to send you one free and give your readers a discount code. No pressure either way."

6. Engagement plan

Respond to every comment and message within a few hours during launch, within a day once things settle.
Ask questions in captions. Repost good customer content. Run monthly giveaways: "Follow us, tag a friend, show us your most-used kitchen item." Use Stories polls and question boxes. Join conversations about sustainable living and home swaps.

7. Paid social

Start small: 10 to 20 dollars a day per platform. Boost posts that already did well organically. Run conversion campaigns during launch weeks. Use lookalike audiences from your email list and website visitors. Retarget people who viewed a product but didn't buy. Run Pinterest ads for gift ideas and room inspiration.

8. Metrics and tracking

Set up before launch: Google Analytics 4, Meta Pixel, TikTok Meta and TikTok Events API, UTM parameters on every link, and a promo code system.

Awareness
- Reach and impressions.
- Follower growth.
- Share of voice: how often people mention you compared with competitors.

Engagement
- Engagement rate: (likes + comments + shares + saves) divided by reach.
- Saves and shares: these show people find the content useful.
- Story replies and poll votes.
- User-generated posts and tagged photos.

Traffic
- Referral traffic from social platforms.
- Email sign-ups from social.
- Profile visits and link clicks.

Sales
- Sales conversion rate: purchases divided by visitors from social.
- Revenue per post and per campaign.
- Average order value and products per order.
- Return customer rate and lifetime value.
- Affiliate sales by creator.

Reporting
- Weekly check-in: what worked, what didn't, one change for next week.
- Monthly report with all metrics and a budget summary.
- A post-campaign review: what you learned about the audience, which creators delivered, what to keep and what to drop.

Launch timeline
- Four weeks out: announce the line, build an email list, tease products.
- Two weeks out: influencer posts go live, paid ads start.
- Launch week: daily posts, a live Q&A, a giveaway.
- Weeks after: turn customer photos into your main content, keep the educational posts going.

prompt: Provide a step-by-step guide on how to care for a wool rug, including the frequency of vacuuming and how to properly spot clean any stains that may occur. Include information on what type of vacuum to use, how to avoid damaging the fibers while vacuuming, and what to do if a spill occurs on the rug. Additionally, provide tips on how to maintain the wool rug's softness and prevent any damage from sunlight or high traffic areas.
completion:
Wool is one of the best natural fibres for a rug. It wears well, resists dirt and repels water, but it still needs regular care. Follow these steps and your rug will stay soft and look good for years.

1. Vacuuming

How often:
- High traffic rooms (entrance, hallway, living room): twice a week.
- Low traffic rooms: once a week is enough.
- Once a month, take the rug outside and give it a good shake, or beat it with a rug beater. This lifts dirt that vacuuming misses.

What vacuum to use:
- A vacuum with a beater bar or brush roll that can be turned off. Wool rugs need suction and a gentle brush. A stiff brush worn down by a motor will felt the fibres, and once wool has felted it stays felted.
- Avoid rotary brush cleaners meant for carpets, and avoid steam cleaners unless the manufacturer says the rug is safe for them.
- If you have a central vacuum, use the setting for bare floors or carpets.

How to vacuum without damaging the rug:
- Turn the beater bar off and use suction only, especially on older or hand-knotted rugs.
- Go slowly. Speed wears the fibres.
- Vacuum in the direction of the pile, not against it.
- Lift the vacuum head when you turn. Dragging it turns the fibres inside out.
- Don't leave the vacuum sitting on one spot with the suction on.
- Empty the canister or change the bag when it's about half full. A clogged vacuum pulls harder and wears the rug more.

2. Spot cleaning stains

Act quickly. The longer a spill sits, the more it sets.

First, work out what the stain is:
- Water-based: juice, coffee, tea, wine, urine.
- Oil-based: butter, grease, makeup, pet oils.
- Tannin: red wine, cola, some fruit juices.
- Protein: blood, milk, egg.
- Dye: ink, paint, hair dye.

General steps for any spill:
1. Blot, don't rub. Rubbing pushes the stain deeper and frays the fibres. Use a clean, dry cloth or paper towel and press down hard. Change the cloth as it picks up the spill.
2. Work from the edge of the stain toward the centre. This keeps the stain from spreading.
3. Use cool water for most spills. Hot water sets protein stains like blood and milk.
4. Test any cleaner on a hidden corner first. Wool takes dye, and some cleaners can lighten it.
5. Let the area dry completely, then vacuum again.

Specific stains:
- Water-based: blot, then dab with a little cool water and a drop of mild dish soap. Blot dry.
- Red wine: blot, then dab with cold water and a little white vinegar (one part vinegar to three parts water). Blot dry. Don't use heat.
- Grease: sprinkle baking soda or cornstarch over it, leave for 15 minutes, then vacuum. Follow with a mild soapy-water dab if needed.
- Blood: cold water only, blotting. If it persists, use a little hydrogen peroxide diluted with water, but test first.
- Urine: blot, then clean with an enzymatic cleaner made for pet urine. These break down the proteins that cause the smell.
- Ink: a little rubbing alcohol on a cloth, dabbing. Test first, because alcohol can lighten some dyed wool.

What not to do:
- No bleach, ammonia or strong all-purpose cleaners.
- No hot water on protein stains.
- No hairdryer or heater to speed drying. Heat shrinks and hardens wool.

3. Keeping the wool soft

- Every few months, use a wool conditioner or fabric softener made for wool. Put a little in lukewarm water, mist the rug lightly, let it sit 10 minutes, then blot dry. Too much softener builds up and attracts dirt.
- If the rug looks matted, fluff the fibres with a wire pet grooming brush or a clean broom, working against the pile, then vacuum.
- Rotate the rug every six months so one side doesn't take all the wear.
- Keep it out of reach of cats' claws. A snagged wool fibre can unravel into a long run.

4. Protecting against sunlight

Sunlight fades and weakens wool over time.
- Close blinds or curtains during the hottest part of the day, especially on south- and west-facing windows.
- If a rug must sit in sun, use an UV-protective film on the window.
- Rotate it regularly so no single patch gets the most light.
- Don't place it directly under a heat lamp or close to a radiator.

5. High traffic areas

- Put a runner or mat in front of the rug in entryways, so the grit that wears wool down stays on the mat instead.
- Grit acts like sandpaper on the fibres, so vacuum the mats as well.
- In very busy spots, ask a professional about a protective treatment. Some will apply a wool-safe protectant that helps repel liquids and dirt.
- If the rug is old or valuable, have it professionally cleaned every 12 to 18 months, sooner if there are pets or children.

6. What to do after a big spill

If a large amount of liquid soaks through:
- Blot up as much as you can with dry towels, pressing hard.
- Put a fan on the area to circulate air.
- Don't sit on the damp spot until it's completely dry.
- If it still feels damp after a day, or you smell mustiness, call a professional. Moisture left in the backing can damage the floor underneath too.

If you tell me the rug's size, where it sits, and what kind of spills happen most, I can make this into a simple weekly routine.
